facts.title: Named After a Tormented King
facts.text: Swedish chemist Anders Gustaf Ekeberg discovered tantalum in 1802 while studying minerals from Ytterby and Finland. He named it after Tantalus, the figure from Greek mythology who was punished by standing in water he could never drink. Ekeberg chose the name because the oxide would not absorb acid even when immersed in it, just as Tantalus could never quench his thirst.

facts.title: A Twin That Caused Confusion
facts.text: For decades scientists believed tantalum and niobium were the same element, because they almost always occur together and behave so similarly. The confusion was only resolved in 1844 by Heinrich Rose, who proved niobium was distinct and named it after Niobe, the daughter of Tantalus, to honour their close relationship. Pure metallic tantalum was not produced until 1903, by Werner von Bolton.

facts.title: Almost Impossible to Melt
facts.text: Tantalum melts at about 3017 degrees Celsius, giving it the fourth-highest melting point of any element, behind only tungsten, rhenium, and carbon. This extreme heat resistance lets it survive conditions that would destroy ordinary metals. It is used in furnace parts, rocket nozzles, and other components that must endure punishing temperatures.

facts.title: The Phone in Your Pocket
facts.text: Tantalum's biggest modern use is in tiny, highly reliable capacitors that store and regulate electric charge. Because tantalum capacitors pack a lot of capacitance into a very small space, they are found in nearly every smartphone, laptop, and games console. A thin self-healing oxide layer on the metal makes these capacitors remarkably stable and long-lived.

facts.title: Friendly to the Human Body
facts.text: Tantalum is exceptionally biocompatible, meaning living tissue does not reject it or react badly to it. Surgeons have used it for decades to make bone plates, cranial repair sheets, dental implants, and stents. Modern porous tantalum, sometimes called trabecular metal, even encourages bone to grow directly into the implant for a stronger bond.

facts.title: Shrugs Off Acid
facts.text: At room temperature tantalum resists attack from almost every acid, including aggressive aqua regia, a mixture that dissolves even gold and platinum. This is because a tough, thin oxide film instantly forms on its surface and shields the metal beneath. As a result it is prized for chemical-plant equipment such as heat exchangers, valves, and reaction vessels that handle corrosive liquids.

facts.title: A Conflict Mineral
facts.text: Most tantalum comes from the ore coltan, short for columbite-tantalite, with major mining in Australia, Brazil, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Because Congolese coltan has at times funded armed groups, tantalum is officially classed as a conflict mineral under regulations like the US Dodd-Frank Act. This has pushed electronics companies to trace and certify the origins of the metal they buy.

facts.title: A Glimpse Inside Atoms
facts.text: Tantalum gave physicists a powerful tool for probing matter through Mossbauer spectroscopy. The isotope tantalum-181 has the narrowest known nuclear gamma-ray resonance line of any element, making it extraordinarily sensitive to tiny changes in its atomic surroundings. This razor-sharp response lets researchers detect minuscule shifts in energy that other elements would miss entirely.

facts.title: Nature's Rarest Stable Isotope
facts.text: Almost all natural tantalum is tantalum-181, but a sliver of about 0.012 percent is tantalum-180m, an excited nuclear state that is the rarest stable nuclide in the universe. Unlike normal excited states that decay in fractions of a second, tantalum-180m has survived for billions of years and has never been observed to decay. How it was forged in stars remains an open puzzle in nuclear astrophysics.

facts.title: Hard, Dense, and Stretchy
facts.text: Tantalum is a dark blue-grey, very dense metal weighing about 16.7 grams per cubic centimetre, roughly twice as heavy as iron. Despite its hardness it is also highly ductile, so pure tantalum can be drawn into extremely fine wire. Combined with hafnium and carbon, it forms tantalum hafnium carbide, one of the highest-melting-point materials ever made at around 4000 degrees Celsius.
